_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V: Asfandiyar's remaining Seven Stages, the Brazen Hold, Rustam and Shaghad. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: The First Stage: Asfandiyar and the Two Wolves
title.zh: 阿斯凡迪亞爾七關之一：雙狼

region.en: Road to the Brazen Hold (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往銅堡之路（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 2

summary.en: Gurgsar warns: two wolves, each like a lusty elephant, a male and female, having horns like stags and all a-gog to make a fight of lions, broad in the neck and breast and thin of flank, with monstrous elephants' tusks, first will confront thee. The prince commits the host to Bishutan and rides to the First Stage; the wolves beheld his breast and neck and his iron mace, and like grim elephants made at him; the hero strung his bow, roaring like a rending lion, and rained arrows down upon those Ahrimans; the steel-tipped shafts disabled both the beasts, and he unsheathed his watered glaive, charged, and hacked their heads, and made the dust mire with their blood.
summary.zh: 古爾格薩爾示警：「首關有雙狼——雄雌各一，大如壯象，鹿角獠牙，獅膽豹心！」王子把大軍託付比舒坦，獨騎赴關；雙狼見其胸膛與鐵錘，如巨象般撲來；英雄獅吼彎弓，箭如暴雨，鋼鏃俱中；他拔出大馬士革利劍衝鋒，斬下狼首，鮮血染塵如泥。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Seven Stages (Haft Khan) of Asfandiyar. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Two wolves, each like a lusty elephant, a male and female, having horns like stags and all a-gog to make a fight of lions, broad in the neck and breast and thin of flank, with monstrous elephants' tusks, first will confront thee, said Gurgsar. Asfandiyar bade lead back Gurgsar bound as he was in miserable plight, and blithe himself assumed his Kaian casque.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief, when he had drawn anigh the wolves, sat firmly like a mighty elephant. The wolves beheld his breast and neck, his waist, his warrior-handgrip, and his iron mace, and like grim elephants and keen for fight made at him from the plain. The hero strung his bow and, roaring like a rending lion, rained arrows down upon those Ahrimans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The steel-tipped shafts disabled both the beasts, and neither could approach unscathed. With joy Asfandiyar perceived them growing weak and sore distressed, unsheathed his watered glaive, and charged. He hacked their heads and made the dust mire with their blood, lit from his noble steed, acknowledging his helplessness to God, and washed the wolves' gore from his arms and person, then sought a spot that had not been defiled upon the sand and, turning toward the sun, exclaimed: O righteous Judge! Thou hast bestowed upon me strength, Grace, process.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Second Stage: The Lion and the Lioness

region.en: Second Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第二段（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 3

summary.en: Upon the next stage lions will assail thee, such as no crocodile would dare encounter; the lusty eagle, valiant though it be, will fly not in their path. There were a lion and a lioness, and bravely both came forth to fight with him, the lion first: he smote it with his sword; its face grew coral-hued; 'twas cloven from head to midriff, which appalled the lioness, yet, like her mate, she came on savagely. The chieftain smote her on the head, which fell and rolled upon the sand; her paws and breast were tulip-hued with blood. He bathed himself and, looking to all-holy God alone as his Protector, said: O righteous Judge! Thou hast destroyed these creatures by my hand.
summary.zh: 第二關有雙獅——「鱷魚不敢近其身、雄鷹不敢掠其頂」！雄獅先撲；他一劍從頭劈至胸膈，獅面如珊瑚綻裂；牝獅不懼，仍凶猛撲上，一錘擊碎其首，頭顱滾落沙中，爪胸染血如鬱金香。英雄沐浴淨身，獨向聖神祝禱：「公義的審判者啊，是祢借我的手誅了這對猛獸！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Upon the next stage lions will assail thee, such as no crocodile would dare encounter; the lusty eagle, valiant though it be, will fly not in their path, said Gurgsar. Tomorrow thou shalt see a valiant man address the lion with the scimitar, answered Asfandiyar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: There were a lion and a lioness, and bravely both came forth to fight with him, the lion first. He smote it with his sword; its face grew coral-hued; 'twas cloven from head to midriff, which appalled the lioness, yet, like her mate, she came on savagely. The chieftain smote her on the head, which fell and rolled upon the sand; her paws and breast were tulip-hued with blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He bathed himself and, looking to all-holy God alone as his Protector, said: O righteous Judge! Thou hast destroyed these creatures by my hand. Meanwhile the troops came up, and Bishutan surveyed the lions' breasts and limbs while all acclaimed Asfandiyar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fourth Stage: The Witch of the Water-side

region.en: Fourth Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第四段（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 5

summary.en: When thou alightest tomorrow at the stage a witch will come to greet thee; she hath looked on many a host, but quailed at none: she turneth waste to sea at will and maketh sunset at mid-day; men call her Ghul. Asfandiyar takes goblet and lute to battle, dight as for a feast, and sings by the fountain's marge; the witch, foul, wrinkled, and malevolent, plies her magic arts amid the gloom and grows beauteous as a Turkman maid, and draws anear with roses in her breast. He possesses a goodly chain of steel which Zarduhst brought down from Paradise for Shah Gushtasp: he flings it around her neck, her strength is gone, she takes a lion's form; within the chain there was a fetid hag, calamitous, and with trenchant sword he smote her on the head.
summary.zh: 第四關的妖巫「古爾」能令沃土化海、白日作暮。王子偏攜酒盃與琵琶赴險，泉邊自歌自飲；巫嫗施法變作麗姝，捧花而至。他早藏著扎爾杜什特自天堂攜來的聖鐵鏈——一鏈套頸，妖力頓消、現出獅形；鏈中蜷伏的仍是那個滿頭白髮、黑面可憎的醜嫗。他揮劍斬其首級，日月為之晦暗。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; pairs with Rustam's witch (persian-rustam-course-witch). No living community restriction.

passages.text: When thou alightest tomorrow at the stage a witch will come to greet thee; she hath looked on many a host, but quailed at none: she turneth waste to sea at will and maketh sunset at mid-day. Men call her Ghul, O Shah! Face not her toil in these thy days of youth. The atheling replied: tomorrow, knave! thou shalt recount my prowess, for I will break the warlocks' backs and hearts, so will I maul that witch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Foul, wrinkled, and malevolent she plied her magic arts amid the gloom and grew as beauteous as a Turkman maid, with cheek as 'twere brocade of Chin and musk-perfumed, of cypress-height, a sun to look upon; her cheeks like rosaries, she drew anear Asfandiyar, with roses in her breast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now he possessed a goodly chain of steel which he had kept concealed from her. Zarduhst, who brought it down from Paradise for Shah Gushtasp, had bound it about the prince's arm. Asfandiyar flung it around her neck; her strength was gone; she took a lion's form. Within the chain there was a fetid hag, calamitous, with head and hair like snow, and black of face; with trenchant sword he smote her on the head, which with her body came down to the dust; sight failed, so loured the sky when that witch died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sixth Stage: Snow, a Spear's Length Deep
title.zh: 七關之六：深可及矛之雪

region.en: Sixth Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第六段（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 7

summary.en: Thou wilt take no thought of mace or bow or sword, and see no opening for fight, no way of flight, for snow, a spear's length deep, will come upon thee, warns Gurgsar. With that there came a fierce blast from the mountains: all the world became like ravens' plumes, and none knew plain from upland; from that dark cloud descended showers of snow; the earth was filled with snow and raging blast, and o'er the desert for three days and nights the fury of the wind was measureless. The tents were soaked through, and not a man could stand or stir for cold; the chief, resourceless, called to Bishutan: make supplication, all of you, to God — and thereon a gentle breeze arose which bare the clouds away and heaven became serene.
summary.zh: 第六關的試煉不是刀兵，而是天災：「雪深及矛、大軍將沒！」和暖春日裡，山間驟起狂飆——天地如烏鴉之羽、不辨丘壑，黑雲瀉雪三日三夜；帳幕浸透、士卒僵立難動。王子束手，命比舒坦率全軍向神祈禱；忽有和風驅散愁雲、天色復明——「真主之門已為我們敞開！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Thou wilt take no thought of mace or bow or sword, and see no opening for fight, no way of flight, for snow, a spear's length deep, will come upon thee, said Gurgsar; a crisis will confront thee, thou with all thy famous army wilt be lost therein.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: With that there came a fierce blast from the mountains, and sore dismayed him. All the world became like ravens' plumes, and none knew plain from upland. From that dark cloud descended showers of snow; the earth was filled with snow and raging blast, and o'er the desert for three days and nights the fury of the wind was measureless. The tents and tent-enclosure were soaked through, and not a man could stand or stir for cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief, resourceless, called to Bishutan: this plight of ours is one with misery. I met the dragon's fumings like a man, but strength and manhood now avail us not. Make supplication, all of you, to God! Then Bishutan made prayer to God, while all the soldiers lifted up their hands, and offered supplications numberless. Thereon a gentle breeze arose which bare the clouds away and heaven became serene, and when the Iranians had taken heart they offered thanks to God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seventh Stage: The Deep River and Gurgsar's Head
title.zh: 七關之七：渡河與古爾格薩爾授首

region.en: Deep river before the Brazen Hold (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 銅堡前的深河（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 8

summary.en: When he had ridden past the troops he saw a deep, unfathomed river, and a camel of the caravan had tumbled in; the chieftain seized and dragged it from the mud. Base villain, said the prince, didst thou not say here thou wilt find no water? He said: thy host's destruction would be as bright to me as sun and moon. The chieftain laughed and promised: when I return victorious from the fight thou shalt be captain of the Brazen Hold — but at the feast Gurgsar curses him: may every evil star control thy life. Roused by his words the prince smote with an Indian sword his head, and clave him, crown to midriff; to the river they flung him presently, and that malignant grew food for fishes.
summary.zh: 第七關是一條無底的深河；馱駱駝墮河，王子竟親手拽其出泥。他質問古爾格薩爾：「你不是說此處無水嗎？」答曰：「你的大軍葬身此地，在我眼中如日月光輝。」王子以王位許諾誘其指路——渡河之後設宴，古爾格薩爾卻咒他「死無葬身之地」。王子怒而揮劍，自冠至膈將其劈為兩半，拋入河中餵魚。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: When he had ridden past the troops he saw a deep, unfathomed river. Now a camel, one of the caravan whose cameleer had kept it in the front, had tumbled in; the chieftain seized and dragged it from the mud, and that malignant Turkman of Chigil quaked. Base villain, said the prince, why hast thou used this snake-like subtlety? Didst thou not say: here thou wilt find no water, and the sun will burn thee up?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He said: thy host's destruction would be as bright to me as sun and moon. I get from thee but fetters; what should I wish but thy bale and loss? The chieftain laughed, stared, was amazed at him, but showed no wrath, and said: Gurgsar, thou man of little wit! When I return victorious from the fight thou shalt be captain of the Brazen Hold; far be from me to harm thee; all the realm is thine if thou wilt give me honest counsel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Gurgsar rejoined: no arrow plumed and pointed, when ironed thus, can find its way across; thou shalt work magic with the mighty stream if thou wilt but unfetter me. The soldiers followed him in single file, inflating at Asfandiyar's behest their water-skins forthwith, and binding them along the barrels of their beasts of burden; they all plunged in, and the host and baggage reached land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Heart-straitened, hostile both in speech and soul, Gurgsar retorted: how long wilt thou use such converse? Be accursed and justly so; may every evil star control thy life, thy waist be cut asunder with the sword, thy gory body flung upon the dust, the earth thy bed, the grave thy winding-sheet. Roused by his words, and raging at the oaf, the prince smote with an Indian sword his head, and clave him, crown to midriff; to the river they flung him presently, and that malignant grew food for fishes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Asfandiyar in the Merchant's Guise at the Brazen Hold

region.zh: 阿爾賈斯普銅堡（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages secs. 9-12

summary.en: I shall approach the hold in merchants' guise, and none will know me for a paladin, says Asfandiyar: ten camels laden with gold, five with brocade of Chin, five with gems, a golden throne and massive crown, eighty pairs of chests with eight score mighty men hidden inside. In slippered feet and blanket, freighted with jewels, he goes toward the hold: a merchant I; my sire was Turkman and my mother Persian. That night a conflagration blazed whose burning scorched the sky; the watchman saw the flames and Bishutan assailed the hold, while within Asfandiyar undid the chest-lids and brought kabab and wine to the men inside, and went boldly to the palace of Arjasp: this merchantman will supply thee with a sword that cost dinars — and Arjasp, a mass of wounds, his huge form sank, and Asfandiyar beheaded him.
summary.zh: 強攻無望，王子改行商賈之計：十馱黃金、五馱錦緞、五馱寶石、八十口暗藏武士的大箱。他趿著便鞋、披著氈毯入城求見阿爾賈斯普：「我是商人，父突厥而母波斯。」入夜，一場大火燒紅了天；比舒坦見煙火為號、揮軍攻堡；箱中勇士破箱而出、開懷暢飲備戰。王子直入王宮，向阿爾賈斯普「獻劍」：「此劍乃魯赫拉斯普所贈，上有古什塔斯普之印——你一接劍，命便歸塵！」混戰中魔王身負重傷，被一劍梟首。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: We might assail this hold in vain for years unless indeed I take upon me to demean myself, and try a stratagem against the foe, said Asfandiyar. I shall approach the hold in merchants' guise, and none will know me for a paladin. Ten of these beasts he loaded up with gold, upon five more he put brocade of Chin, another five had various kinds of gems, a golden throne and massive crown. He brought forth eighty pairs of chests, and made choice of eight score of his mighty men, and, having hidden them within the chests, bound on the baggage and set forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages secs. 9-10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: With slippered feet, a blanket thrown about him, and freighted with the jewels, gold, and silver, the chieftain went in haste toward the hold, and journeyed in the guise of chafferers. May wisdom mate with kings! a merchant I: my sire was Turkman and my mother Persian; I purchase from Turan, bear to Iran, and deal in stuffs, in clothes, and furniture, in jewels, crowns, and other valuables.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 10 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The night came and a conflagration blazed, whose burning scorched the sky. When from the look-out the watchman saw the flames by night he left his post and came exultingly to Bishutan, and told what he had seen of fire and fume. The army from the plain approached the hold; when news spread in the hold that a host hath come the place rang with the name Asfandiyar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asfandiyar, when night was growing dark, arrayed himself again in fighting-gear, undid the chest-lids that more air might come to those inside, and brought kabab and wine with other provand. And, clutching with his hand a glittering sword, cried to Arjasp: now will this merchantman supply thee with a sword that cost dinars; I give it as a present from Luhrasp. They closed in strife outrageous, foot to foot with sword and dagger; Arjasp failed 'neath the blows; he was a mass of wounds; his huge form sank, and then Asfandiyar beheaded him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pitfalls of Kabul and the Fall of Rakhsh
title.zh: 喀布爾陷阱與拉赫什之墜

region.zh: 喀布爾獵場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 3

summary.en: The king of Kabul honeycombs the chase with pits, arranging them beneath the rides, and in them sets haft-downward hunting-spears, swords, double-headed darts, and scimitars, and masks the openings so that neither man nor eye of beast might see them. The king comes out bare-footed, dust on head, his heart all guile, and begs pardon of Rustam, who forgives him and hunts on the plain below the city. Rakhsh sniffs fresh earth, spins like a ball, and shies, suspicious of the smell, and tears the ground to pieces with his iron shoes; howbeit that fleet steed picked his steps right warily so as to make his way between two pits — but Rustam's heart is filled with wrath at Rakhsh, and he lashes him; two of his feet go through; the haunches of the mighty Rakhsh, and Rustam's legs and bosom, are impaled.
summary.zh: 喀布爾王在獵場密掘陷阱，坑中倒插獵矛、寶劍與雙頭鏢，覆以偽裝；又跣足頂塵、假意乞憐，騙得魯斯塔姆原諒而入獵。忠馬拉赫什嗅出新土、如球般後旋刨地——牠機警地想從兩坑之間踏過；魯斯塔姆卻誤怪戰馬、揚鞭催行——兩蹄落空，巨馬的後臀與英雄的腿胸一齊被坑中利刃刺穿！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the death of Rustam by treachery. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Now when ill-starred Shaghad had left Kabul the monarch hurried to the hunting-ground, and took a hundred sappers, men of note among the troops. They honeycombed the chase with pits, arranging them beneath the rides, and in them set haft-downward hunting-spears, swords, double-headed darts, and scimitars, and made a shift to mask the openings that neither man nor eye of beast might see them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bare-footed, dust on head, his heart all guile, he went before the chief, who pardoned him his fault. There was hard by the city of Kabul a pleasant, fertile spot with wood and water, and there they willingly encamped. When thou wouldst hunt, said the king, I have a district where on plain and hill game throngeth; wild sheep, onager, gazelle fill all the waste.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rakhsh sniffed fresh earth, spun like a ball, and shied, suspicious of the smell, and tore the ground to pieces with his iron shoes. Howbeit that fleet steed picked his steps right warily so as to make his way between two pits; but Rustam's heart was filled with wrath at Rakhsh, and fortune veiled discretion from his eyes. He raised his hunting-whip and lashed Rakhsh; two of his feet went through; he had no purchase; all below was spear and sword; and so the haunches of the mighty Rakhsh, and Rustam's legs and bosom, were impaled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam's Last Arrow Pins Shaghad to the Tree
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆臨終一箭釘死逆弟

region.en: Hollow plane-tree of the hunt (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獵場空心梧桐樹（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 4

summary.en: Since such an ill hath come on me, says dying Rustam, uncase my bow for me, and let it serve as mine interpreter: it is not fit that lions on the prowl shall see me fallen here and sorely wounded. Shaghad draws near, uncases the bow, and laughs exulting at his brother's death; the matchless hero clutches it, and Shaghad, in terror at those arrows, skulks behind a hollow plane-tree. Rustam puts forth his hands, sore wounded as he was, and looses a shaft: he pins his brother and the tree together, and gladdens in the article of death — now God be praised, that even when my soul hath reached my lips day hath not turned to night o'er my revenge. He spake, his soul departed from his body, and all the folk bewailed him bitterly.
summary.zh: 垂死的英雄命逆弟為自己解弓上弦：「莫讓巡行的獅群見我重傷倒地。」笑看兄長垂死的沙加德怕那兩支箭，閃身躲進一棵空心梧桐樹後。魯斯塔姆強提餘力放箭——一箭連人帶樹釘穿！臨終他歡然謝神：「縱然魂至唇邊，天也未在我復仇之前轉為黑夜！」言畢魂散，舉世同悲。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Warner notes Firdausi chose the treachery version over Bahman's revenge raid. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Since such an ill hath come on me uncase my bow for me, and let it serve as mine interpreter, said Rustam; string it and lay it by me with two arrows. It is not fit that lions on the prowl, and coming on the plain in quest of quarry, shall see me fallen here and sorely wounded. Shaghad drew near, uncased the bow, and strung it; he drew it once, then laid it down by Rustam, and laughed exulting at his brother's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The matchless hero clutched it lustily, though tortured by the anguish of his wounds, what while Shaghad in terror at those arrows made haste to shield himself behind a tree, an ancient plane still boughed and leaved but hollow, and there behind it skulked the miscreant. When Rustam saw this he put forth his hands, sore wounded as he was, and loosed a shaft: he pinned his brother and the tree together, and gladdened in the article of death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shaghad, when he was stricken, cried out Ah! but Rustam had not left him time to suffer, and cried: now God be praised, and I have known Him through all my years, that even when my soul hath reached my lips day hath not turned to night o'er my revenge, but He hath given me strength before my death to wreak me on this traitor. He spake, his soul departed from his body, and all the folk bewailed him bitterly; within another pit Zawara died; remained no horseman high or low beside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Shaghad sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
